title: Leon Black fails to appear for House deposition on Epstein ties; sues to block subpoenas
dek: Leon Black, a financier with documented ties to Jeffrey Epstein, did not appear September 3 for a scheduled House Oversight Committee deposition. Black filed a federal lawsuit the same day seeking to block two congressional subpoenas demanding he produce nondisclosure agreements and testify about his relationship with Epstein.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Black's defiance and legal challenge represent a high-stakes test of congressional subpoena power against a wealthy defendant with resources to litigate, setting up a constitutional clash as Congress races against the end of the legislative session.
bottom_line: A federal judge must decide whether the House Oversight Committee's subpoenas exceed its delegated authority, a ruling that could either validate or constrain congressional power to investigate wealthy individuals. The outcome will likely determine whether the committee can obtain the NDAs before the 119th Congress ends and whether Comer or his successor will pursue contempt charges.
body:
Billionaire financier Leon Black did not appear on Thursday, September 3, 2026, before the House Oversight Committee for a scheduled deposition about his ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The same morning, Black filed a federal lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia seeking to block two congressional subpoenas: one demanding he produce nondisclosure agreements and another requiring him to testify.
The move represents a direct challenge to the committee's investigative authority and sets up a constitutional test of congressional power as Congress approaches the end of its session.  According to the Senate Finance Committee, Black maintained a social relationship with Epstein since the mid-1990s and paid him more than $170 million for tax and estate planning advice. Black's name has appeared repeatedly in Justice Department releases of Epstein files, including a poem attributed to Black in a collection of birthday messages sent to Epstein that was released by the House committee last year.
Black first appeared before the committee in June 2026 for a transcribed interview, but testimony ended abruptly after members from both parties said Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. On June 26, 2026, James Comer, the Republican chair of the Oversight Committee, issued two subpoenas to Black: one demanding he produce all nondisclosure agreements to which he is a party, and another requiring him to appear before the committee again. In August 2026, in a letter to Black's attorney, Comer threatened to hold Black in contempt if he refused to comply.
In his lawsuit, Black's lawyers argue that the two subpoenas are invalid to the extent they exceed the committee's delegated authority in seeking private information unrelated to a legitimate legislative purpose. The filing also contends that compliance would expose women who value their privacy, have no known or public connection to Epstein, and have refused to release confidentiality agreements. Black's attorney Susan Estrich stated: "The Committee is on a fishing expedition that oversteps its authority and completely ignores its responsibility. This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr. Black."
Black's legal team has reiterated his denials. According to a statement released Thursday: "We want to reiterate that Mr Black had no awareness of the criminal activities that led to Epstein's arrest in 2019. Mr Black never abused a woman. He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein." Before his June appearance, Black maintained that he was unaware of Epstein's criminal activity until 2019 and paid Epstein only for legitimate services in part due to Epstein's unrivaled network of relationships with influential figures. Black's financial payments to Epstein served as a lifeline to the convicted sex offender in the years after Epstein's 2008 prison sentence.
On Thursday morning, Comer criticized Black, stating: "It's a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people. Our deposition is moving forward this morning for the record and there will be an empty chair for Mr Black. I will speak with our members about next steps." After Black filed the suit and failed to appear, Comer signaled that the committee may move to hold Black in contempt of Congress but said he wants to gain consensus and examine the legal path ahead before proceeding. Comer told reporters: "I would hold him in contempt right now. Of all the powerful billionaires and political people we brought in for interviews and depositions, this is the first time anyone's filed suit."
Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, called for Black to be held in contempt after his refusal to appear. Garcia stated: "By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two congressional subpoenas. His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable. We must hold him in contempt immediately."  Both Comer and Garcia believe Black is attempting to run out the clock as time runs short on the 119th Congress, complicating the committee's effort to conclude its investigation before the session ends. Comer told reporters: "Obviously, we're running up against the clock at the end of this Congress. I'm sure his legal team knows that. So we've got to be smart from here on in." Garcia responded: "What he's trying to do is to slow the process down of getting us the information. He's very aware that Comer no longer is going to be the chairperson. But what Mr. Black should understand is that we will be even more aggressive than Chairman Comer as it relates to his testimony."
Earlier in the week, over a dozen survivors of Epstein's abuse urged Black to comply with congressional subpoenas, writing: "Black's use of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein's orbit. If Black continues to withhold responsive records or refuses to comply with the committee's demands, Congress should use every tool available to enforce its subpoenas." Other figures who have appeared for the investigation include former Democratic President Bill Clinton, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates.
